findings.title: Mercy beside the womb image
findings.claim: The focus's mercy name can carry a distant generative image: 22:5 describes life held in wombs through its formation and brought out at birth, giving the mercy phrase a possible sheltering, life-forming resonance.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is the focus epithet ar-Raḥīm at 1:1:4:2. The independent trigger is 22:5's explicit womb image and its sequence from gestation to birth. Their shared r-ḥ-m pattern meets an image of an inner vessel holding life to a term; this lets the focus's ordinary mercy reading acquire a possible generative-enclosure shade.
findings.reader_payoff: Mercy can be perceived as a life-holding relation as well as a divine quality.
findings.containment: The focus has a masculine mercy adjective, while 22:5 has the plural anatomical noun al-arḥām. This is a root-level contextual image, not a claim that ar-Raḥīm lexically means womb or that God is bodily enclosed. The source-side counterevidence calls the route root-only and unclarifying, so the reading remains exploratory and secondary to ordinary mercy.

epistemic.reason: The supplied target Arabic gives an explicit womb and developmental sequence, but supplies no target morphology; its reciprocal source-direction record is negative, so the proposed return through the focus remains a bounded root resonance.

findings.title: Mercy as active rescue
findings.claim: The paired mercy names can be heard as active beneficence in relation to loss: 2:64 makes Allah's favor and mercy the explicit condition for not being among the losers, while 6:12 names mercy as written upon Himself before gathering and then mentions those who lost themselves.
findings.mechanism: The carriers are the two mercy epithets at 1:1:3:2 and 1:1:4:2. The independent trigger in 2:64 is an explicit conditional relation between Allah's favor and mercy and not being counted among the losers; 6:12 places mercy, gathering, and lost selves in one wider sequence. These contexts make the focus's mercy legible as active beneficence in relation to loss, with 2:64 providing the direct causal statement.
findings.reader_payoff: The mercy names gain a concrete relation to human ruin: mercy is shown as what can keep people from becoming losers.
findings.containment: This does not claim that 2:64 comments on 103:0 or that both passages describe the same event. It extends the focus's attributive mercy reading through an explicitly supplied wider relation; it does not replace it.

epistemic.reason: The exact supplied Arabic in 2:64 states the causal contrast, while its source-direction note calls the overlap indirect; 6:12 supplies adjacency rather than an explicit causal claim, and target morphology is absent.

findings.title: The name as a means of invocation
findings.claim: The focus's phrase bi-smi Allah can be heard as invocation through a divine name: 17:110 and 7:180 explicitly direct people to call upon Allah or call upon God through His names.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is ism in the focus phrase at 1:1:1:2. The independent triggers are 17:110's instruction to call Allah or ar-Raḥmān and its reference to God's beautiful names, and 7:180's command to call Him by those names. The focus's ordinary name relation meets an external act of address, changing the phrase from a bare identification into an invocation-bearing opening.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the name in the basmala as a way of turning toward the named one, not only as a label attached to Him.
findings.containment: The focus remains a prepositional phrase with the name in the genitive; the target verses' direct-call syntax is not transferred to it, and no specific request is supplied by the basmala itself.

epistemic.reason: Both external texts explicitly connect divine names with calling, but their target morphology is absent and the focus has a different local syntax.

findings.title: The formula at thresholds of speech and action
findings.claim: The same basmala phrase appears within Solomon's letter and Noah's boarding instruction, while another verse ties mention of Allah's name to eating; these uses let the focus's opening formula accompany consequential speech and action.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is the focus's full bi-smi Allah, ar-Raḥmān, ar-Raḥīm relation. The independent triggers are the letter identified as Solomon's in 27:30, the imperative to board in 11:41, and the instruction to eat from what Allah's name has been mentioned over in 6:118. The formula's return within those distinct acts makes the focus phrase read as an enacted opening under the named one, not only as a heading.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the basmala as a phrase that can orient a message or undertaking at the moment it begins.
findings.containment: These wider uses do not prove that the focus's local occurrence refers to a letter, voyage, or meal. They illustrate how the same formula can accompany speech and action while the ordinary invocation remains intact.

epistemic.reason: The supplied target texts show the repeated formula and surrounding acts directly, but target morphology is not supplied and the functional synthesis remains an inference across contexts.
